content: The updated guidelines for the use of antiretroviral drugs are a significant advancement toward achieving the global goal of universal access to antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for both the treatment and prevention of HIV. This aligns with the ultimate objective of ending the HIV epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030. The recommendations in these guidelines are categorized as follows: 1. New Recommendations (2016): These are newly introduced and published for the first time in these guidelines. They address new areas of focus or replace previous recommendations. Supplementary web annexes provide evidence supporting these recommendations. 2. Existing Recommendations (Unchanged in 2016): These were published in earlier WHO guidelines and remain unchanged. The source of the original guideline is cited, and the evidence base is included in the original source document. 3. Existing Recommendations (Reviewed and Updated in 2016): These were published in earlier WHO guidelines but have been reviewed and updated for this edition. Supplementary web annexes include evidence supporting these updates. Any changes to the strength of the recommendation are noted in the relevant chapter. Retesting Prior to Enrollment in Care WHO advises national programs to retest all newly diagnosed individuals with HIV using a second specimen and a second operator, following the same testing strategy and algorithm, before enrolling the client in care or initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). This applies regardless of whether ART initiation depends on CD4 count. Retesting individuals already on ART is not recommended due to the potential risks of incorrect diagnosis, particularly with in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) that use oral fluid specimens. Preand Post-Test Services Guidelines emphasize the importance of privacy protection and the establishment of policies, laws, and norms to prevent discrimination and promote the rights of people living with HIV. This creates an environment where disclosing HIV status becomes easier. Principles and Approaches for Service Delivery Lay providers who are trained and supervised can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Provider-initiated HIV testing and counseling (PITC) should be offered in all clinical settings, especially for clients presenting with symptoms or conditions indicative of HIV infection, such as tuberculosis (TB) or malnutrition. HIV Diagnosis in Infants and Children HIV serological assays used for clinical diagnostic testing should have a minimum sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98% under quality-assured laboratory conditions. HIV virological assays for infants (usually at or after six weeks of age) should have a sensitivity of at least 95% and specificity of 98% or more. HIV virological testing is strongly recommended for diagnosing HIV in infants and children below 18 months of age. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or at the earliest opportunity thereafter. ART should be initiated immediately for infants with an initial positive virological test result, while a second specimen is collected to confirm the result. Timing of Virological Testing Adding nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth to existing early infant diagnosis (EID) testing approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants. Point-of-Care Technologies NAT technologies validated for use at or near the point of care can be used for early infant HIV testing. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV serology can be used to assess HIV exposure in infants less than four months of age. Provider-Initiated HIV Testing and Counseling for Infants and Children In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics should be routinely tested for HIV. HIV testing should also be offered in outpatient or immunization clinics. Other Priority Populations Adolescents from key populations should have access to HIV testing services linked to prevention, treatment, and care. Pregnant women in high-prevalence settings should undergo routine PITC as part of antenatal, childbirth, postpartum, and pediatric care. HIV-negative pregnant women should be retested during the third trimester, postpartum, or during labor due to the high risk of acquiring HIV during pregnancy. Couples and partners should be offered voluntary HIV testing services with support for mutual disclosure. Diagnostics In high-prevalence settings (HIV prevalence >5%), a diagnosis of HIV-positive should be provided to individuals with two sequential reactive tests. In cases of discrepant test results, the client should return for retesting within 14 days. In low-prevalence settings (HIV prevalence <5%), testing strategies should be adjusted accordingly.
